archetype.name: Playoff Team (offense-first)
archetype.definition: A Lions team whose top-five passing attack and elite pass rush win most weeks, while a leaky coverage unit keeps it a notch below the true contenders.

report.headline: An elite passing offense is carrying a defense that only rushes the passer.
report.take:
This is Dan Campbell's fifth straight Lions team with a top-10 offense by EPA. History has it 6th in 2022, 8th, 3rd, 9th last year, and 7th now. The 2026 version is driven by Jared Goff, who has started every game, and the passing game ranks 3rd in pass EPA and 3rd in success rate. Amon-Ra St. Brown is the target hog with 97 looks. Jahmyr Gibbs is the engine on the ground with 222 carries and is also a real receiving option with 58 targets. The run game is better than its raw EPA suggests: 4th in run success and 7th in yards before contact. It also gets stuffed too often, 27th in stuff rate and 27th in short yardage.

The defense is a strange, lopsided unit. It ranks 30th in EPA allowed and 27th against the pass, yet it is 2nd in sacks with 36 on the season and tackles better than anyone, 1st in missed-tackle rate. The pass rush wins its downs. The coverage behind it loses the in-between ones. It is 27th in EPA on short passes, 31st against tight ends and 27th on third down. With only 8 takeaways (25th), it rarely flips a drive on its own. Offenses know it: teams pass against Detroit more than against almost anyone, 2nd-strongest pass funnel in the league.

The 8-2 record runs a bit ahead of the play. Net EPA sits 16th, and an 80% win rate in one-score games (3rd) did a lot of lifting in narrow wins over New Orleans, Green Bay and Minnesota. Last year's 0.375 one-score rate shows how fast that can turn. Still, this is no mirage. The point differential of +68 implies about 7.1 wins, and the Lions add hidden margin with the 3rd-best special teams and a perfect fourth-down go rate. The real caveat is the recent defensive surge. Holding opponents to 15, 9 and 10 points came against offenses now ranked 30th, 28th and 13th, and the early-season tape against better passers (410 yards allowed to New Orleans, 329 to Carolina) is just as real.

Where it heads: Detroit and Chicago are tied at 8-2, they meet twice in the final six weeks, and every remaining division game after Thursday is on the road. The offense is a known, durable quantity. The ceiling of this team depends on whether the pass defense can hold up against good quarterbacks, not just pile up sacks against weak ones.

strengths.title: Top-five efficient passing attack
strengths.body: Goff is running one of the league's most efficient passing games, 3rd in pass EPA and 3rd in offensive success rate. It rests on a line that is 5th in pressure rate allowed and on a target tree that runs through St. Brown, Gibbs and the tight end. Four straight seasons of top-10 offense say this is structural, not a hot streak.

strengths.title: A pass rush that wins every week
strengths.body: Detroit is 2nd in sacks and 4th in sack rate, and it has gotten home multiple times in nearly every game. It is the reason a bottom-tier coverage unit survives. Drives die on negative plays rather than on stops in coverage. Sack production is reasonably sticky, though it depends on the defense being healthy up front.

strengths.title: Hidden yardage and aggression
strengths.body: Special teams rank 3rd in EPA per game, and Campbell has gone for it on every fourth-down opportunity the model flags. Both add a quiet edge in field position and possessions. That matters for a team living in one-score games, and both are coaching-driven and likely to last.

concerns.title: Coverage leaks underneath and to tight ends
concerns.body: The defense is 27th in pass EPA allowed and 27th on short throws, and tight ends have feasted, 31st in EPA per target to TE1s. This is a real flaw, not a role cost. Quarterbacks get rid of the ball before the rush lands and pick on the middle of the field. Safety Chuck Clark's hamstring could make it worse.

concerns.title: Third downs and no takeaways
concerns.body: Opponents convert 44.4% on third down (27th) and score touchdowns on two-thirds of red-zone trips (22nd). The defense also has only 8 takeaways (25th). Without turnovers or get-off-the-field stops, the offense has to match long drives score for score. That makes the margin thin against good offenses.

concerns.title: Close wins outrunning the efficiency
concerns.body: An 80% one-score win rate (3rd) sits on top of a net EPA that ranks only 16th. The point differential implies about a win fewer than the record shows. Last season's swing to a 20th-ranked one-score record shows this tends to regress, so the margin for error late in the year is thinner than 8-2 looks.

trend.note: Detroit hasn't lost since early October, and the defense went from allowing 300-plus passing yards in four of the first five games to 129-210 lately. Some of that came against weak offenses like Minnesota, Miami and Tampa Bay. The offense dipped against Minnesota's top-ranked defense and in Miami, then rebounded with strong passing EPA against New England and Tampa Bay.

nextGame.headline: Thanksgiving tiebreaker: Goff's deep shots against Chicago's elite short coverage
nextGame.body:
Two 8-2 teams meet indoors in Detroit on a short week, with first place in the NFC North on the line. The Book has Chicago a 2.5-point road favorite, and the 55.5 total expects points. Chicago's defense is a mirror image of Detroit's offense in one key way. It suffocates short passes (2nd in short EPA) and third downs (1st), but it is 31st in EPA on deep throws. Chicago's offense leads the league in time of possession and holds the ball longest before throwing, which gives Detroit's 2nd-ranked sack unit time to get home. The Bears' profile includes three non-Caleb Williams starts early, so their offense is probably better than its 11th-ranked EPA with him back. They are also 29th in turnover margin despite an 8-2 record and the 4th-most wins over expected, so they have been fortunate too.

Availability leans against Detroit on the back end. Starting safety Chuck Clark (91% of snaps) missed Monday's walkthrough with a hamstring. Edge DJ Wonnum (back) and DT Skyler Gill-Howard (knee) are questionable, and backup corner Ennis Rakestraw Jr. is out. On offense, Sam LaPorta (ankle) was limited and is questionable, and center Cade Mays is on injured reserve. Chicago will be without slot corner Kyler Gordon, which loosens its coverage. Tackle Theo Benedet is questionable, a possible opening for the Detroit rush.

waysToWin.title: Push the ball vertically
waysToWin.body: Chicago takes away the underneath game but bleeds big plays deep, and it is down Kyler Gordon. Goff and Jameson Williams can trade completion percentage for chunk gains. A couple of explosive completions flip a game in which Chicago is otherwise efficient.

waysToWin.title: Feed Gibbs against a soft spot
waysToWin.body: Lead backs have done well against Chicago, which ranks 30th in EPA per play allowed to RB1s and 29th in fantasy points over average. Gibbs as a runner and receiver keeps Detroit ahead of the sticks. That steers the offense away from Chicago's 1st-ranked third-down defense.

waysToWin.title: Sack the quarterback who holds it
waysToWin.body: Chicago's quarterbacks hold the ball longer than any team's, and Detroit's rush is among the league's best at finishing. Sacks and pressured throws are the Lions' best shot at the takeaways they rarely get, against an opponent already 29th in turnover margin.

waysToLose.title: Third downs and sacks stall drives
waysToLose.body: Chicago is 1st on third down and 2nd in sack rate, while Detroit is only 19th in sack rate allowed and is playing without its injured center. If the deep shots don't land, the Bears' rush can turn third-and-medium into punts. That is the formula Minnesota's defense used to hold Detroit to 19.

waysToLose.title: Chicago's clock-eating drives
waysToLose.body: The Bears lead the league in time of possession, and Detroit's defense is 27th on third down. Long, methodical drives would shorten the game and leave a short-week Lions offense with too few possessions to win a shootout.

waysToLose.title: A thin secondary gets picked apart
waysToLose.body: If Clark can't go, an already shaky coverage unit loses its most-used safety and Rakestraw's depth on a four-day turnaround. Detroit is 31st against tight ends and 27th on short passes. Quick throws that beat the rush are exactly how Chicago can neutralize the Lions' best defensive weapon.

nextGame.watch: Whether Goff takes early shots deep against Chicago's 31st-ranked deep coverage, or settles for the short throws the Bears smother.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense is the dependable part. It has been top-10 for years, and its passing efficiency and pass protection should keep scoring near the top of the league. The defense's recent run of single-digit and mid-teens games should regress somewhat once it faces better quarterbacks, since the coverage and third-down numbers haven't changed. The close-game win rate is also likely to cool. The pass rush and special teams are real and travel.

The schedule splits in two. Atlanta and Tennessee are games Detroit should win. Then come Minnesota's top-ranked defense on the road, the Giants, and road trips to Chicago and Green Bay to close. A playoff berth is likely. The division title, and whether this is more than a one-and-done playoff team, comes down to the two Chicago games and whether the secondary gets healthy.
swingFactors: Split of the two Chicago games
Chuck Clark's and the secondary's health

confidence.note: Ten games is a fair sample. Recent defensive gains came against weak offenses, and the close-game record is volatile.
